display.text: Using observed patterns to choose a hypothesis or test direction and then treating that choice as if it had been specified beforehand.
Samples linked across conditions so their observations cannot be treated as independent between groups; matched pairs are a common example.
The result of subtracting one measurement from its matched measurement in a specified order, yielding one numerical observation per pair.
The population parameter μ_d, the average paired difference, equal to μ₁ − μ₂ for differences defined as measurement 1 minus measurement 2. The sample mean difference estimates it.

An interval of plausible values for μ_d, the population mean paired difference. Its sign must be interpreted using the stated subtraction order; a matching two-sided test rejects zero when zero lies outside it.
The sample mean difference minus the null mean difference, divided by s_d/√n. With the usual zero null, t = d̄/(s_d/√n).

A one-sample t-test applied to paired difference scores, usually testing H₀: μ_d = 0. Different pairs must be independent; small-sample exact inference assumes normal differences. Also called matched-pairs t-test.
The sample spread s_d of paired difference scores around their own mean; it is not the difference between the two conditions' standard deviations.
For n independent pairs, the estimated sampling spread of their mean difference: s_d/√n, where s_d is the SD of within-pair differences.
